newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran says holds haj rally in defiance of Saudi ban.
newsitem.headline: Iran says holds haj rally in defiance of Saudi ban.

text.p: Iran said on Monday its pilgrims held a rally denouncing the United States and Israel in Islam's holy city of Mecca in defiance of a Saudi ban on political activity during the haj pilgrimage.
The official Iranian news agency IRNA said the rally, which Iran calls "disavowal of infidels", was held on Sunday despite the heavy presence of Saudi police aiming to stop the rally.
The rally drew pilgrims from Iran, Lebanon, Pakistan, Kuwait, Tunisia, Palestinian territories, Algeria and Libya, said the agency, monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation.
"There is no God but Allah, America is the enemy of God and Israel is the enemy of God," IRNA quoted pilgrims as chanting.
There was no word from Saudi Arabia on the reported rally.
Iran had said it postponed the rally scheduled for Saturday to avoid confrontation after Saudi forces were deployed in front of the Iranian haj offices in Mecca to prevent it.
Tense relations between Saudi Arabia and Iran usually take a turn for the worse over the staging of the rally during the annual haj, which this year reaches a climax on April 16.

Radical Shi'ite Iran says Moslems should air political grievances during the haj, mainly through rallies to denounce Israel and the United States as enemies of Islam. Sunni Saudi Arabia says the pilgrimage is purely religious and should not be politicised.

The row between the Gulf's two richest oil states has resurfaced at every haj since 1987, when 402 people, mostly Iranians, died in clashes with Saudi security forces at an Iranian-led rally. Iran boycotted the haj for three years.
Saudi Arabia had said it would deal harshly with violators of the ban on political activity during haj.
To avoid confrontation with Saudi security, Iranian pilgrims in recent years staged low-key rallies within Iran's haj compounds and Saudi forces did not interfere.
Iran is trying to improve relations with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf Arab states and its officials and state media have in the run up to haj been using softer tones towards the kingdom.
About two million Moslems, half from outside Saudi Arabia, are expected to perform this year's haj at Mecca, site of Islam's holiest shrine.
